sections.h2: What to do with the 21-7-13 tail: eight practices
paragraphs: These are the author’s own exercises, drawn from the logic of the triad — not a ritual and not a guarantee of results.

ol: **The voice behind you.** Before any “that’s it, enough” decision, ask yourself three questions. What am I really ending right now? Who will fall along with it? What will I think about this in a year? This is the voice that rode behind the victor in a Roman triumph. Nobody will assign one to a person with 21-7-13, so you have to say it to yourself.

**The slow rider.** No irreversible endings on the day the decision ripens. Write it down, set a date a week later, and if it hasn’t changed, carry it out — announced, not as a blow. Waite’s Death rider moves slowly, and this is not weakness: it is how an ending gets room.

**A yellow card.** Make a deal with yourself to speak about your unhappiness while it is small: “this is hard for me”, “I don’t want it to go on like this”. The rule is simple: no ending without a warning. This is Strength that does not stay silent until the lightning.

**A limit in advance.** At the start of any risky venture, write down the condition under which you will end it: a deadline, a sum, a sign. When the condition arrives, the ending becomes keeping a promise to yourself, not surrender. This exercise is for the Reviver.

**A rite of ending.** When something ends — a job, a stage, a relationship, a city — mark the ending: a last day, words of thanks, a short review of “what I take with me, what I leave, what was alive here”. There is a rose on Death’s banner, and every ending has something worth carrying on.

**Bring it to the wreath.** Once a week, finish one small thing completely and celebrate the completion itself, not a victory. The World’s wreath surrounds the figure; it does not sit on her head. The tail needs to know the joy of an ending in which nobody lost.

**The lion, not the world.** When you want to reshape your circumstances — quit, move, cut someone off — first ask: what in me is demanding this right now? Sometimes the answer is that it is time to leave. Sometimes it is time to rest, to say something unpleasant, or to admit you are tired. Strength rules the lion, not the world around it.

**The sun between the pillars.** After any ending, leave yourself an in-between season — a time when the old has finished and the new has not yet begun. In Wen the rider heads towards the rising sun, “though that sun is still far in the distance”. A new big plan a week after an ending is usually the same chariot on a new road.

paragraphs: The signs that the practice is working are modest and easy to check. Your departures stop being a surprise to others. You can say hello to former colleagues and partners. You can stop a losing venture before it eats everything. After an ending you don’t rush straight into a new assault.

sections.h2: The strength of 21-7-13: a master of transitions
paragraphs: In its lived-through version 21-7-13 gives a rare and much-needed gift — the ability to end things. Most people are afraid of endings and drag them out for years. A person with this tail is not afraid of them. The World lets them see the whole and bring it to completion. The Chariot gives them the strength to go through a transition rather than get stuck in it; the first meaning of this card in Waite’s list is “succour”. Death teaches that after an ending life goes on in another form.

People like this close companies so that nobody is left without money or a next step. They part in a way that does not turn the children into a battlefield. They move without tearing up their roots. They guide others through loss and change, because they know that road themselves. Wen writes that Death can mean the overthrow of a former authoritarian regime, and calls it “the card of revolutions”. A lived-through 21-7-13 has no need for revolutions: they change the order of things before it starts to crush anyone.

Waite remarks that the explanations of the thirteenth card are “on the whole, better than usual”: rebirth, creation, destination, renewal. That is the mature work of this tail. Not destruction and not killing, but an ending after which something is born.

And the Roman triumph suggests one last formula. There is no need to give up victories: the World and the Chariot are strong cards, and a person with 21-7-13 really does know how to win. All that is needed is someone riding behind the victor and saying: look behind you, you are human, and everything, your victories included, has its term. This is not a threat. It is exactly what keeps a victory alive.

sections.h2: What this article is based on

ul: **Calculation** — Natalia Ladini’s classic destiny matrix scheme with points A–T: D = A + B + C, E = A + B + C + D, M = D + E, N = D + M; every sum over 22 is reduced by adding its digits. The “13 or 49” rule was checked by running every day from 1900 to 2100. The frequencies, the distribution by year, month and day, the constant points of the chart, the purposes and the absence of the triad in other lines were counted over all dates from 1900 to 2025.

**Card meanings** — A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, 1922 reprint) and Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015). Both are quoted in the original English. The numbering follows Waite: 8 is Strength, 11 is Justice, 22 is the Fool.

**Other sources**: Tertullian, “Apology”, ch. 33 (the words spoken to the man in triumph); Plutarch, “On Tranquillity of Mind”, ch. 4 (Alexander’s tears); Descartes, “Discourse on the Method”, part III (the third maxim of morals). These quotations are in our translation.

**The names “The Destroyer and Killer” and “Destruction, Death to Many Souls” and the past-life legends** are taken from popular interpretations of the destiny matrix. Neither Waite nor Wen wrote about the matrix or karmic tails. Assembling the three cards into a script, reading the Chariot as the hand that does Death’s work, the three faces of the tail, the role of Strength in the centre and the reading of the purposes are the author’s interpretation.
The destiny matrix is an esoteric model for self-observation with no scientific evidence base. It is not a forecast, not a diagnosis and not advice on health, money or relationships.

faq.q: What happened in the past life of a person with the 21-7-13 tail?
faq.a: Popular interpretations tell different stories: an executioner, a jailer or a merciless warrior; a ruler, an inventor of weapons or a revolutionary whose decision changed the fate of many; a person who took their own life too early. These are legends of the tradition: neither numbers nor cards establish the events of past lives. It is more useful to read them as a description of what can be seen already now — a habit in which an ending comes not in its own time but by force.

faq.q: Does “The Destroyer and Killer” mean that I am dangerous, or that death is threatening me?
faq.a: No. The name is an image, not a description of character and not a forecast. Waite’s Death card speaks of a change in the form of life, and he himself considers rebirth and renewal its best explanations. Popular guides sometimes contain threats like “if you don’t work through your tail, you’ll die before your time”. There is no basis for them either in the cards or in the method. Numbers predict neither illness, nor death, nor violence.

faq.q: Are 21-7-13 and 13-7-21 the same tail?
faq.a: Yes, if we are talking about the bottom ray of your chart. In this scheme a tail cannot start with 13: its first number is always a multiple of three. And in other lines and chakras the triad 13-7-21 does not occur at all. So 13-7-21 is your 21-7-13, read from the bottom corner towards the centre. The meaning is read in the direct order: the entry is the World, the mechanism the Chariot, the root Death.

faq.q: I have arcanum 13 at 60–70 on the age scale. Is that dangerous?
faq.a: No. For everyone with 21-7-13, point D falls on the decade from 60 to 70, and Death stands there. The age scale does not set lifespans: an arcanum describes the theme of a period. For Death that theme is a change of form — a different rhythm, a new role in the family and at work, the completion of a big stage. It is worth meeting it the same way as any ending in this tail: in advance and without armour.

faq.q: How is 21-7-13 different from 3-7-22?
faq.a: They share a mechanism, the Chariot, and a centre, Strength. Everything else is different. 3-7-22 starts with the Empress and goes down to the Fool at the root: it is the tail of a home that becomes a fortress, and of a freedom that needs no escape. 21-7-13 starts with the World and goes to Death: it is the tail of a victory that lacks the skill of ending. 3-7-22 is twice as common: 2.9% of dates against 1.5%. With the 3-13-10 tail, 21-7-13 shares only Death, and there it stands in the middle, not at the root.

faq.q: Is 21-7-13 different for women and men?
faq.a: No. Gender plays no part in the calculation and changes neither the numbers nor the mechanism. Advice like “a woman should soften, a man should stop fighting” is stereotype, not a conclusion from the cards. The Destroyer, the Reviver and the Runaway are found in everyone.

faq.q: Is the 21-7-13 tail the same as the “21-7-13 program”? And in a compatibility matrix?
faq.a: A karmic tail is the M–N–D triad on the bottom ray. Many websites also call the tail itself a program; then it is the same thing. In the other lines of a personal chart the triad 21-7-13 never occurs. In a compatibility matrix the numbers are calculated from two dates, and the same triad then describes the couple’s script, while each partner keeps their own personal tail. The article above is about the personal chart.

faq.q: What if a child has 21-7-13?
faq.a: Teach them to finish things, not just to win. To stay till the end of the season before dropping an activity. To say goodbye to what is going away: an old school, a move, belongings. Show by your own example that an ending can be announced in advance and calmly. And don’t make love a reward for victories: a child with the Chariot in their tail needs to know that losses and endings can be survived.

faq.q: Can the 21-7-13 tail be “closed”?
faq.a: The numbers in the matrix do not change — what changes is how the script plays out. Signs of a tail lived through: people know about your endings in advance; you can stop a losing venture without feeling defeated; after you leave, people can still say hello; you have time between the old and the new; you don’t need a victory to feel that it was all worthwhile.

report: Popular destiny matrix guides call the karmic tail 21-7-13 “The Destroyer and Killer”, yet the person who carries it is often the most patient one in the room. For years they take the blows, then one ordinary Tuesday hand in their resignation and leave every work chat the same day. To everyone around, it is a bolt from the blue: “but he never said anything”.

The name is explained by a past-life legend: an executioner, a ruler, an inventor of weapons, a person who took their own life too early. None of these versions can be checked: a birth date tells nothing about events in the past. But the legends share a common denominator more interesting than any of them: in each, the end comes not in its own time but by force.

That is how the tail is built. In the middle stands the Chariot, and Waite’s divinatory list gives it “succour, providence; also war, triumph, presumption, vengeance”. At the root is Death, whose list opens with “end, mortality, destruction”. The folk lists did not invent the word “destroyer”: it can be put together from two neighbouring cards.

report.h3: Death needs no sword

report: But the roles in this pair are cast unexpectedly. Waite describes the charioteer as “carrying a drawn sword”, while the rider on the Death card “carries no visible weapon”, and yet everyone falls before him, from king to child. **Death needs no sword. A sword is for whoever has taken on Death’s work.**

So this is how we read the name: the “destroyer” here is not Death but the Chariot, which has decided to end things itself. And “killer” is not about people but about endings: the habit of breaking off relationships, projects and ties with one’s own hand instead of letting them end.

report.h3: A triumph deaf to the whisperer

report: After a great victory, a Roman general rode into the city in a triumphal chariot, wearing a laurel wreath. Tertullian records a detail: from behind, someone kept telling the man in triumph, “Look behind you! Remember that you are a man.” Later retellings turned these words into memento mori — “remember that you will die”.

Waite knew nothing about the destiny matrix, yet he calls the Chariot “the King in his triumph” and says of Death that it is “more especially a card of the death of Kings”. The tail unfolds between these two phrases, and the voice from behind is here too: it is the root. The whole script is a triumph in which nobody hears the whisperer.

It begins with a hunger for the whole. At the entry stands the World, for Waite “the perfection and end of the Cosmos”. Half is never enough for a person with this tail: work means being the best at it, love means forever. But the whole cannot be taken; it can only be put together or lived through. And the Chariot can do only one thing: win.

In Wen the World is encircled by “the wreath of victory”, and her charioteer also wears “the laurel wreaths of victory”. But in the World the wreath embraces a dancing figure, while in the Chariot it sits on the head of a man in armour. **A whole to live inside becomes a trophy to wear.** Work turns into a siege, love into a conquest.

Then the ending comes: a project is exhausted, a feeling has cooled, the city has become foreign. The last word among the Chariot’s reversed meanings in Waite is “defeat”, and that is how the charioteer hears any ending. He has three moves. The Destroyer gets ahead of the ending and finishes everything himself. The Reviver fights for what has already died. The Runaway leaves before it becomes clear that everything is over. All three moves rest on one belief: **the end must be my action**, anything but an event that simply happened.

report.h3: The longer Strength holds on, the harder the Tower strikes

report: The riddle of the patient destroyer is solved in the centre of the chart. Everyone with 21-7-13 has Strength there, the comfort zone. Wen boils it down to a formula: “Compassion is strength.” The Chariot masters the world around it; Strength masters the self.

And in Manipura, the chakra of will, status and money, everyone with this tail has the triad 8-8-16: Strength, Strength again and the Tower. While Strength holds the lion, tension builds up unnoticed, then comes out in a single discharge, and the decision is carried out at the Chariot’s full speed. Waite calls the Tower “a card in particular of unforeseen catastrophe”, and of Death’s rider he writes that he “moves slowly”. The tail mixes up these two cards of ending. **An ending that could have come like a sunset reaches others like lightning.**

The decision is often right; the form is wrong. Nobody gets to say goodbye, and mutual friends are crossed out with the relationship, good colleagues with the job. This is the everyday sense of the tail’s second folk name, “death to many souls”: when the Destroyer ends one thing, everything around it ends too.

report.h3: The sword is one detail too many

report: The numbers point the way out. The entry is the sum of the root and the centre: 21 = 13 + 8. The World is Death plus Strength, the ability to end things plus a gentle hand. This is a play of numbers, not a proof, but an exact one: here the whole is put together not by victories but by endings. Waite compares the World’s garland to “a chain of flowers”, the lion of Strength is led on a chain of flowers, and on Death’s banner there is a rose, the sign of life. Only the Chariot has no flowers: there the charioteer carries a sword.
The task is to learn to end things without a sword. The author’s exercises, drawn from the logic of the triad, not a ritual:

ul: The voice behind. Before any “that’s it, enough”, ask three questions: what am I really ending, who will fall along with it, what will I think about this in a year? Nobody will assign a whisperer to a person with 21-7-13.
The slow rider. No irreversible endings on the day the decision ripens: set a date a week later and, if the decision holds, carry it out in the open, not as a blow.
No ending without a warning. Speak up about unhappiness while it is still small. This is Strength that does not stay silent until the lightning.
An in-between season. After an ending, leave a pause before anything new begins. A new big plan a week later is usually the same chariot on a new road.

report.h3: A victory with someone riding behind it

report: Lived through, 21-7-13 gives a rare gift: the ability to end things. Such a person closes a company so that nobody is left without a next step, parts without turning the children into a battlefield, and guides others through loss, because they know that road themselves. Waite finds the explanations of the thirteenth card “on the whole, better than usual”: rebirth, creation, destination, renewal.

There is no need to give up victories: a person with 21-7-13 really does know how to win. All that is needed is someone riding behind the victor, reminding him to look back: he is human, and everything, his victories included, has its term. This is not a threat. It is exactly what keeps a victory alive.

items.title: Karmic tail 3-13-10 in the destiny matrix: prune, don’t uproot

seo.title: 3 13 10 in the destiny matrix: a karmic tail without scare stories
seo.description: Tail 3-13-10: the Empress, Death and the Wheel. Why the “suicide” label is wrong, who has this tail, every birth date with it, and how to work with it.

items.short: The karmic tail 3-13-10 is the scenario of a gardener who grows living things generously, but at the first change of season doesn’t prune them — he pulls them up by the roots. The Empress at the entry (M) gives the desire to create, Death in the middle (N) turns every transition into a final ending, and the Wheel of Fortune at the root (D) teaches you to pass through a change of phase without losing the harvest. This is not a “suicide programme”, as popular lists frighteningly call this tail: it is about how a person ends projects and relationships, not about the end of life. The tail is rare — 149 birth dates since 1900 — and it always comes with the centre 20, Judgement.

paragraphs: If you boil it down to one thought: Death in this tail is not a misfortune that befalls what was created, but the habitual way a person closes stages themselves. Working through the tail does not mean you stop ending things. It teaches you to end a part, not the whole.

sections.h2: Why 3-13-10 is called “Suicide”, and what is wrong with that label
paragraphs: In popular lists, the 3-13-10 tail is labelled “Suicide” or “the Suicide”. Then usually come stories about a soul that “failed to cope in a past life”, about a weak instinct for self-preservation and a choice “between life and death”. The label is put together mechanically: the Empress is life, Death is death, the Wheel is fate, so the total is “a life cut short by one’s own hand”. If you have come here after such a reading — especially a reading of your child’s chart — breathe out. This conclusion does not follow from the arcana themselves.

In The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, Arthur Edward Waite writes of the thirteenth card as change of form and passage “from lower to higher”. On his horseman’s banner is the Mystic Rose, “which signifies life”, and between the pillars on the horizon shines “the sun of immortality”. He finds the existing explanations of the card better than usual on the whole: “rebirth, creation, destination, renewal”. Waite does not strike the theme of death out of the card, but neither his book nor Benebell Wen’s modern Holistic Tarot gives any grounds for predicting death or misfortune from the arcanum. And a karmic tail in the Arcana Sense scheme does not assign events at all: it describes a habitual pattern that repeats.

The frightening label does have an honest grain of truth, and it is worth naming directly. This scenario has a difficult place — the pause between the end of one form and the start of the next. The old is already over, the new not yet planted, and the empty field can feel heavy: “I don’t feel like doing anything”, “it was all for nothing”. This is not a sentence and not a character trait but a phase, discussed in detail below.

If thoughts of death are not a symbol from the matrix but something that is happening to you or someone close to you right now, you need to talk to a living person, not to the arcana. Call your local emergency number or a local crisis line — crisis lines talk to children, teenagers and parents too.

sections.h2: The scenario: grow, uproot, start again
paragraphs: Waite calls the Empress the door or gate by which an entrance is obtained into this life, and an image of universal fecundity: a field of corn is ripening in front of her, and beyond there is a fall of water. In the 3-13-10 tail she stands precisely at the entry. So the circle begins not with a problem but with a rise: an idea, a person, a project, a home appears — and you want to grow all of it. Such a person starts out of desire, not duty. People and resources gather quickly around their idea, and the first fruits appear sooner than other people’s.

Then the season changes. There is nothing catastrophic about this; it is how all living things live: a project needs rules and a different scale, falling in love needs agreements, a grown child needs a different distance, a team needs new roles. At such a moment a gardener prunes branches, moves the plant to a bigger pot, thins something out. In the weak version of 3-13-10 a different reflex kicks in: if the old form no longer fits, then everything is over. And the plant is pulled up by the roots.

Then the Wheel turns and a new season comes: a new field, a new idea, a new rise. The person is generous again, grows things fast again — and at the next change of form again puts a full stop where a comma would have done. After a few turns a familiar feeling appears: “everything starts beautifully for me and always ends the same way”. Wen writes of the Wheel as a card under which history repeats itself and the past becomes the future, down to a sense of déjà vu. For this tail, déjà vu is the most accurate signal that the circle has started another turn.

paragraphs.h3: What uprooting looks like, and what repotting looks like

head: Where
How the tail works
What the way out looks like
rows: close the project when it has outgrown the “garage” format and needs procedures
change the format: hire people, delegate, keep the product and the clients
quit as soon as the role changes or a new manager arrives
discuss the new role and bring into it what you did best
break up when falling in love gives way to everyday life
rework the agreements on time, money, duties and intimacy
quietly disappear from a group that has changed
change how often you meet and keep the people you still feel warmly about
abandon and delete a piece that you’ve “stopped liking”
finish the series, set the draft aside, start the next part
move and start from scratch, giving things away, instead of renovating
remake the space for a new stage of life

paragraphs: There is neither cowardice nor whim in the left-hand column. There is decisiveness that has mistaken a stage for the whole.

sections.h2: What keeps the circle going: relief that feels like a revelation
paragraphs: Death in position N is the mechanism that makes the repetition stable. Its mature work is to end what has outlived itself and free up space. In the tail this work is overdone: instead of one dry branch, the whole tree goes. And things immediately feel easier. You don’t have to endure the in-between stage, where the old no longer works and the new has not yet taken shape. You don’t have to watch a beautiful beginning turn into a complex system. Relief fixes the circle in place more reliably than any belief. Wen herself links Death with the darker aspects of the Wheel of Fortune: change you don’t control and a transition you resist.

3-13-10 has a second support too, invisible if you look only at the tail’s three numbers. This tail only arises with a matrix centre of 20 — Judgement (how this works is explained in the section on arithmetic). Waite describes Judgement as a response to a call heard from within: something in us sounds a trumpet, and all that is lower rises in response — “almost in a moment, almost in the twinkling of an eye”. Wen calls this card an epiphany: all the evidence is on the table, the judgement has been made.

In our reading, it is this link that explains why the break in 3-13-10 doesn’t look like running away. The person doesn’t slip off into something new, as in the neighbouring tails with the same entry — they pass a verdict. The decision “that’s it, enough” comes all at once, feels like clarity, almost like an awakening, and so seems unconditionally right. Sometimes it really is right. But the feeling of revelation doesn’t prove the verdict correct: the trumpet can sound out of tiredness, too, or out of fear of the transition. Time helps to tell one from the other — more on this in the practical part.

sections.h2: The second trap: numbness after the ending
paragraphs: In Waite’s list of divinatory meanings, the thirteenth card has “end … destruction”, and reversed, “inertia, sleep, lethargy”. A calculated number has no reversed position, but the pair itself is telling: a transition can be failed in two ways — by cutting it off too early, or by getting stuck after the end. In her reading of the reversed card, Wen describes the second option as a plateau: the person feels it is time to move into a new phase and cannot budge.

In 3-13-10, numbness often follows the break. The garden has been uprooted, the field is empty, and a new desire has not yet come. The Empress is the ability to want and to grow, so the empty field is felt especially sharply: a person used to living from one idea to the next suddenly wants nothing. This, apparently, is where the gloomy interpretations of the tail come from.

The Wheel at the root gives a direct answer: winter is a phase, not the end of the garden. “What goes up will come down. What hits bottom will bounce up,” Wen writes of the tenth arcanum. It helps the holder of 3-13-10 to know a simple thing about themselves: emptiness after an ending happens to them, and it passes. It doesn’t have to be filled at once with a new start, and it shouldn’t be taken as the truth about life. If it drags on and grows heavier, that is a reason to talk to a psychologist, not to look for answers in the matrix.

sections.h2: The root task: stay on the wheel instead of jumping off
paragraphs: Position D is the root task the whole circle keeps returning to. Here stands the Wheel of Fortune. Waite sees in it the perpetual motion of the world and the flux of human life, and in the sphinx at the top of the wheel, the equilibrium within this motion. He specifically notes that seating the sphinx on a fixed pedestal above the wheel spoils the symbol: the meaning of the card is stability amidst movement, not apart from it. And one more of his thoughts: behind the turns of the wheel stands not chance but Providence.

For 3-13-10 this is a ready-made statement of the task. You can’t stop the wheel: the Empress will grow things anyway, and what grows will change form anyway. Jumping off at every turn, as the tail’s Death does, is no way out either. The task is to become someone who stays themselves while the forms change: “this form is over, but the story goes on”. Then the experience of the previous round passes into the next one instead of burning up with the old shell.

In practice, the Wheel teaches you to tell phases apart. Any living undertaking has sowing, growth, a plateau, pruning and winter. A plateau is a pause in growth, not its end. Pruning is care for the tree. Winter is not emptiness for ever. A person with 3-13-10 most often mistakes two difficult but ordinary phases for the end — the plateau and the pruning. Learning to name the phase out loud is already half the work.

sections.h2: How to prune instead of uprooting: practice
paragraphs: The ability to put a full stop is a strength of this tail, and there is no need to give it up. The task is narrower: to end stages, not everything at once. Below are six techniques, each answering a specific link in the circle.

What exactly has stopped working? What of what you have created is still valuable? What next form could it move into? If all three questions have concrete answers, the decision looks like pruning. If there is only one answer — “I want this to be gone” — it is most likely relief talking, not clarity.

Before any ending, write down what you are taking with you: skills, people, money, texts, groundwork, conclusions. The Empress does not grow things so that everything burns. If the inventory comes out empty, you are probably leaving too early: the harvest hasn’t been gathered yet.

A decision to end things comes as a revelation, so let it sit. Say it out loud to someone you trust, set a date and come back to it in a few days. Real clarity will survive the pause; a rush of relief usually won’t.
Find the smallest ending that will relieve the tension: close one role, one format, one commitment, one project out of five. Often this is enough for the tree to start growing again.

When a stage really is exhausted, end it completely: say thank you, hand things over, settle debts and agreements, say goodbye. A break leaves things unsaid, and it is exactly from that unsaid that the numbness after the ending grows. A good ending is Death in its mature form: a horseman with a rose on his banner, not an explosion.

When the feeling “this has happened before” appears in a new situation, stop. This is the place where the circle repeats and where it is easiest to break: make at least one move on this turn differently from the previous ones.

sections.h2: Arithmetic and rarity: what sets 3-13-10 apart among the 26 tails
paragraphs: In the Arcana Sense scheme, the tail is calculated like this: D is the reduced sum of the day, month and year arcana, the centre E is the sum of all four, then M = D + E and N = D + M. Any number over 22 is reduced by adding its digits. For 3-13-10 the arithmetic adds up to an almost narrative picture: the Wheel and Judgement give the Empress (10 + 20 = 30, reduced to 3), and the Wheel and the Empress give Death (10 + 3 = 13). Death in the middle is literally the sum of the root and the entry.

This can be read as a hint — as our interpretation, not a rule of the method. Death here is not an outside force that takes away what you created. It is made of two of your own qualities: what you grow, and the fact that every living thing goes through phases. The meeting of growth with a change of season is inevitable; the only choice is whether it becomes pruning or uprooting.

Add the day arcanum (numbers up to 22 are taken as they are; for 23–31, the sum of the digits), the number of the month and the year arcanum (the sum of the digits of the year; if over 22, add the digits again). If you get exactly 10, your tail is 3-13-10. If you get 28, 37, 46 or 55, the Wheel also stands at the bottom of your chart, but the tail is different: 21-4-10. For example, 4 January 1949: 4 + 1 + 5 (1 + 9 + 4 + 9 = 23, then 2 + 3) = 10.

A sum of exactly 10 requires all three terms to be small, so the tail is rare. From 1 January 1900 to the start of October 2026, 149 dates out of 46,298 give it — 0.32%. That makes it the third rarest of the 26 tails the formula produces; only 9-18-9 and 6-14-8 are rarer. The 21-4-10 tail also has the root 10, and it is about 27 times more common.

Two more features follow from this. The 3-13-10 tail only occurs in people born between 1 January and 1 July. And more than half of the matching dates — 88 of 149 — fall in 2000–2024. There are no such dates at all before 1949, and after 1 January 2024 the next one will not come until 4 January 2030.

paragraphs.h3: Every birth date with the 3-13-10 tail

head: Years of birth
Dates
rows: 5 January, 23 January, 4 February, 3 March, 30 March, 2 April, 1 May
6 January, 24 January, 5 February, 23 February, 4 March, 31 March, 3 April, 30 April, 2 May, 1 June
